clue.text: Mistress seen in many books

definitions.meaning: Mistress ... is one of the two scheming wives in Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor
a leaf of a book, one side of a sheet, which every book has many of

explanation.surface: A kept woman turns up as a character in plenty of novels.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's Merry Wives of Windsor calls its heroines Mistress Ford and Mistress Page, so 'Mistress' alone can give the surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The first sense is a Shakespearean wife's surname; the second is a leaf side, which any bound volume contains by the hundred.

clue.text: Where Tancred ruled, at loggerheads with old church

parts.note: being against something is being anti it

explanation.surface: A crusader's city was in conflict with the ancient Church.
explanation.walkthrough: Tancred, a leader of the First Crusade, was regent of the principality based on this Syrian city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norman crusader Tancred governed this city as regent of its principality in the early twelfth century.

clue.text: Would-be architect's irritation after dreadful delay with winch

indicators.note: after places the irritation word behind the jumbled letters
dreadful says the following words are in a terrible state, so their letters are jumbled

parts.note: used as anagram fodder
used as anagram fodder
irritation is anger

explanation.surface: An architect fumes at a slow crane on site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dreadful' scrambles DELAY and WINCH into EDWINCLAYH; 'after' puts ANGER behind them. 'with' only joins the two fodder words. The definition's 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnold Bennett's hero of the novel named after him longs to become an architect but is made to join his father's printing business.

clue.text: A Tolkien character seen in Chorley? That's odd in a clear way

indicators.note: seen in places the Tolkien character inside the rest of the wordplay
odd says the town's letters are set out strangely, an anagram

parts.note: a Lancashire town, used as anagram fodder
the Ents are the tree-herding giants of The Lord of the Rings

explanation.surface: Someone wonders why a Lord of the Rings figure would turn up in a Lancashire town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' gives COHERLY, which 'seen in' opens up. Chorley is a town in Lancashire, England; 'That's' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking with coherence means expressing ideas logically and lucidly, which is to say clearly.

clue.text: A kind of butterfly, symbolically

parts.note: names a butterfly species whose name is also a punctuation symbol, the white mark on its wing having that shape

explanation.surface: A butterfly described in terms of a printed sign.
explanation.walkthrough: The butterfly carries a small white mark under its wing shaped like the punctuation symbol it is named after.
explanation.definitionFit: This orange-brown butterfly is named for the curved white mark on its hindwing, like the mark separating clauses in writing.

clue.text: Beckett's statement of the situation

parts.note: a phrase summing up the state of affairs that is also the title of a Samuel Beckett prose work

explanation.surface: A dramatist sums up the state of affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Beckett's 1961 novel, Comment c'est in French, has a title that is an everyday phrase describing the way things stand.
explanation.definitionFit: The everyday phrase describes the present state of affairs, and Beckett used it as the title of a late novel.

clue.text: One responsible for Falstaff's riotous entry in costume

indicators.note: in puts the jumbled letters within the costume word

parts.note: a robe is a costume or gown

indicators.note: riotous says the letters run wild, an anagram

parts.note: used as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A fat knight bursts on stage in a gown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'riotous' gives ERTNY, which 'in' places in the costume. Falstaff here is the 1976 novel, not Shakespeare's character.
explanation.definitionFit: This English poet and novelist wrote Falstaff, a novel narrated by Shakespeare's fat knight.

clue.text: Model a politician hunts in a tragicomic trilogy about relationships

parts.note: a norm is a model or standard
an is the form of the indefinite article before a vowel
a Con is a Conservative politician
quests are searches or hunts

explanation.surface: A fashion model and an MP go searching for something within a play cycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' gives AN, the other form of the indefinite article. CON is short for Conservative, Britain's party of the right.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Ayckbourn's trilogy of comic plays shows one weekend of family entanglements from three rooms of a house.

clue.text: With good following, the French crime writer

indicators.note: following puts the letter for good after the other pieces

parts.note: les is the French plural definite article
a sin is a wrongdoing or crime

explanation.surface: A French detective novelist gets a favourable sequel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' puts the good letter last. 'crime writer' tempts as one phrase, but crime is wordplay: the writer is Doris or Gotthold Ephraim.
explanation.definitionFit: Doris Lessing, Nobel laureate, and the German dramatist Gotthold Lessing both bear this surname as authors.

clue.text: Novel with a student author showing absurd brat's wisdom and wit

indicators.note: absurd says the words are made nonsense of, an anagram

parts.note: used as anagram fodder, the possessive adding no letter
used as anagram fodder
used as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A book by an undergraduate displays a spoilt child's sense and humour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'absurd' rearranges BRATS, WISDOM and WIT; 'and' only joins the last two.
explanation.definitionFit: Flann O'Brien's comic novel is narrated by a Dublin student who is writing a novel of his own.

clue.text: Reform nugatory son of a Gunn

indicators.note: reform tells us to make the word over into a new shape, an anagram

parts.note: used as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A worthless son of a family needs to change his ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reform' rearranges NUGATORY. Neil M. Gunn, the Scottish novelist, wrote Young Art and Old Hector.
explanation.definitionFit: In Neil Gunn's novels the boy hero is called this, a child of the fictional Gunn creation, punningly the author's offspring.

clue.text: With reference to other facts

parts.note: re means concerning or with reference to
alia is Latin for other things

explanation.surface: A phrase about further information.
explanation.walkthrough: ALIA is Latin, as in 'inter alia' (among other things).
explanation.definitionFit: The word means real things or actual objects, as opposed to representations, so facts in a loose sense.

clue.text: Phil, very much attached to an old schoolteacher

parts.note: taken as written
lots means a great deal, very much
on can mean attached, as a lid is on

explanation.surface: A man called Phil is very fond of an elderly teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'attached' gives ON, as something stuck on is attached; 'to' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Phillotson is the village schoolmaster in Hardy's Jude the Obscure who marries Sue Bridehead.

clue.text: Russian playwright's giant Russian revolutionary, short of time but grasping victory

parts.note: OS stands for outsize, so very large

indicators.note: grasping says the shortened name holds the victory letter
short of means lacking one of the time letters

parts.note: Leon Trotsky, the Bolshevik leader

explanation.surface: A huge Bolshevik, pressed for time, still snatches a win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short of' leaves TROSKY, and 'grasping' makes TROVSKY. OS means outsize. The 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander Ostrovsky was the nineteenth-century Russian dramatist best known for The Storm.

clue.text: Workplace provided for a telegraphist in Victorian London — about time!

definitions.text: Workplace provided for a telegraphist in Victorian London

parts.note: C stands for circa, Latin for about
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry that the Victorian telegraph office was overdue.
explanation.walkthrough: C is circa, about, as before a date. Victorian telegraph clerks worked in enclosed booths behind grilles.
explanation.definitionFit: A Victorian telegraph clerk worked inside a barred enclosure, like a bird in its coop.

clue.text: God of peace, in a fight reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means as heard spoken, so a word that sounds the same

parts.note: a fray is a fight or brawl

explanation.surface: A god of peace somehow ends up in a brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reportedly' wants a word that sounds like FRAY, a fight.
explanation.definitionFit: In Norse myth this Vanir deity governs peace, fertility, sunshine and prosperity.

clue.text: Echo instructions about a notorious pirate

parts.note: re means about or concerning
Edward Teach was the pirate known as Blackbeard

explanation.surface: Orders about a famous buccaneer.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Teach (or Thatch) was Blackbeard, the early-eighteenth-century pirate.
explanation.definitionFit: To give a lesson again is to repeat the instruction, echoing what was taught before.

clue.text: Literary Glaswegian doctor's vehicle is scratched, going round old bit of medieval Spanish city

indicators.note: going round places the shortened vehicle around the other pieces
scratched means removed, so the word is is struck out

parts.note: the TARDIS is the time machine of Doctor Who

indicators.note: bit of takes only the first letter of medieval

parts.note: Leon is a city in northern Spain, once a medieval kingdom

explanation.surface: A Scottish writer's doctor finds his car damaged near an old Spanish town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scratched' leaves TARD, and 'going round' wraps it round the rest, M coming from 'bit of medieval'. The 's means 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Leonard was a Glasgow poet famous for verse written in the speech of the city's working class.

clue.text: Can an honest style of play get you somewhere in Monopoly?

parts.note: may means can, as in having permission
fair play is honest play, so fair

explanation.surface: Will playing straight win you the board game?
explanation.walkthrough: On the British Monopoly board, MAYFAIR is the most expensive property, a smart district of central London.
explanation.definitionFit: In the London edition of the board game this upmarket district is the costliest square.

clue.text: Refuge for the French to be surrounded by grass

indicators.note: surrounded by says the French verb sits inside the grass word

parts.note: to grass is to inform, so a grass is an informer, a rat
etre is French for to be

explanation.surface: A Frenchman seeks shelter in a field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grass' is British slang for an informer. 'surrounded by' holds French 'to be' inside; 'for' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: A hideaway or safe place one withdraws to is a sanctuary, a place of shelter.

clue.text: Almost finish arresting informer or conspirator's helper

indicators.note: arresting means catching hold of, so the informer word is held inside
almost says the last letter is left off

parts.note: to stop is to finish
a rat is an informer

explanation.surface: Police nearly done with catching a grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' leaves STO, which 'arresting' holds round the informer. In Julius Caesar, Strato holds the sword on which Brutus dies.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, Strato is the servant who helps Brutus, a leading conspirator, to kill himself.

clue.text: Old character almost burns breakfast dishes

indicators.note: almost means the old letter's name loses its last letter

parts.note: yogh is an obsolete Middle English letter
a burn hurts, so hurts here means stings or burns

explanation.surface: An elderly person nearly scalds himself at the breakfast table.
explanation.walkthrough: YOGH, a letter of Middle English, loses its final H through 'almost' to give YOG.
explanation.definitionFit: These cultured milk foods in pots are often eaten in the morning meal.

clue.text: Joy about book that provided income for Rev W. Awdry?

definitions.text: that provided income for Rev W. Awdry

indicators.note: about says the joy word goes round the book letter

parts.note: glee is joy

explanation.surface: Delight at a book that earned the creator of Thomas the Tank Engine his money.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rev W. Awdry, creator of Thomas the Tank Engine, was a parish clergyman, so his living may have included church land.
explanation.definitionFit: Glebe was a piece of land attached to a benefice, its rents supporting the parish clergyman.

clue.text: Victorian poet exalted by a lexicographer

parts.note: august means dignified or exalted
taken as written
Noah Webster compiled the American dictionary

explanation.surface: A nineteenth-century poet is praised by a dictionary maker.
explanation.definitionFit: This English poet and dramatist of the 1860s to 1890s is noted for dramatic monologues and feminist essays.

clue.text: Ruddy old actor that's seen in a Chekov performance?

parts.note: cherry describes a bright red, ruddy colour
Sir Herbert Beerbohm Tree was a great Victorian actor-manager

explanation.surface: A red-faced veteran thespian appears in a Russian play.
explanation.walkthrough: Chekhov's last play is The Cherry Orchard, so its stage is full of such things. 'that's' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Chekhov's play The Cherry Orchard is set around an orchard, so its scenery features such fruiting trees.

clue.text: Producer of Three Chinese Poets using some Chinese themes

indicators.note: using some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A translator of classic verse draws on a few oriental motifs.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'ChineSE THemes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Vikram Seth, the Indian novelist, translated Wang Wei, Li Bai and Du Fu in his book of that title.
